title: EU Company APAC Engineering Hub Setup Guide: SG, TW & HK Compared
summary: Step-by-step EU company APAC engineering hub setup guide comparing Singapore, Hong Kong, and Taiwan on talent cost, entity structure, IP protection, and timelines.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** EU companies can establish an APAC engineering hub in Hong Kong, Singapore, or Taiwan within 14–16 weeks using a hybrid EOR-to-entity approach. Start with an Employer of Record for immediate hiring while incorporating a local subsidiary in parallel, then transition employees to direct payroll once the entity and bank account.


---


Picture this: it's 18 months from now, and your Berlin-based CTO reviews a pull request submitted at 6 PM Hong Kong time — just as she arrives at the office at 10 AM CET. Your APAC engineering hub has shipped three major product features this quarter, your blended engineering cost is 38% lower than your Munich benchmark, and your IP sits safely under a jurisdiction with bilateral protections aligned to EU standards. That's what a well-executed EU company APAC engineering hub setup guide should get you to.

Now let's work backwards through every decision, every trade-off, and every operational detail that gets a European company from intent to a functioning APAC engineering team.


## Prerequisites: What You Need Before You Start


Before committing budget or signing any contracts, European companies need clarity on three fronts. Skipping these prerequisites is the single biggest reason APAC hub launches stall at month four.


### Define Your Engineering Scope and Headcount Trajectory


Are you building a feature team (5–12 engineers) or a full product engineering hub (25–80+)? The answer changes everything — entity structure, office requirements, and management overhead. Map out your 12-month and 36-month headcount targets. According to Deel's 2024 State of Global Hiring report, the average APAC engineering team scales from 8 to 22 people within 18 months of establishment. If your three-year plan doesn't exceed 15 engineers, an Employer of Record (EOR) model may be all you need.


### Confirm Your IP and Data Residency Requirements


EU companies operating under GDPR have specific obligations around data processing and transfer. Before selecting a jurisdiction, consult with your DPO about Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and whether your engineering work involves processing EU citizen data. Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and Singapore's PDPA both have adequacy mechanisms that work with GDPR frameworks, but Taiwan's PDPA requires more careful structuring — particularly for health or financial data.

### Secure Internal Sponsorship and Budget Approval


This sounds obvious, but I've watched three European scale-ups burn six figures on exploratory trips and legal consultations without C-suite alignment on the "why." Your business case needs three numbers: target cost savings (typically 30–45% on blended rates versus Western Europe), time-to-market improvement from timezone coverage, and the break-even timeline. For most mid-market EU companies, break-even on entity setup costs lands between month 10 and month 14.


## Step 1: Select Your APAC Jurisdiction


This is the highest-leverage decision you'll make. Singapore, Hong Kong, and Taiwan each serve different strategic profiles.


### Singapore — The Default Choice (and Why That's Not Always Right)


Singapore ranks first in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business index for APAC and offers English as a working language, strong IP courts, and a deep fintech/enterprise SaaS talent pool. The Economic Development Board of Singapore reports that over 4,000 European companies have regional HQs there. But the trade-off is cost: a mid-level software engineer in Singapore commands SGD 7,000–12,000/month (approximately EUR 4,800–8,200), according to the 2024 Robert Half Salary Guide. Office space in the CBD runs SGD 9–12 per square foot. If cost arbitrage is your primary driver, Singapore's advantage over Western Europe is narrower than many EU CFOs expect.


### Hong Kong — Timezone Overlap and Financial Infrastructure


Hong Kong sits at UTC+8, giving EU teams a 5–7 hour overlap window with CET during standard working hours — more than enough for daily standups and synchronous code reviews. Corporate tax is capped at 16.5%, and there's no withholding tax on dividends paid to EU parent companies. The talent pool skews toward full-stack and infrastructure engineering, with strong representation from mainland China graduates. A mid-level engineer in Hong Kong costs HKD 35,000–55,000/month (EUR 4,100–6,500), per the 2024 Hays Asia Salary Guide. Where Hong Kong excels is speed: company incorporation takes 4–7 business days through the Companies Registry, and opening a corporate bank account (the real bottleneck) can be done in 2–4 weeks with proper documentation.


### Taiwan — The Deep Tech Talent Arbitrage


Taiwan's engineering talent pool is disproportionately strong in embedded systems, semiconductor-adjacent software, and systems programming. TSMC's gravitational pull means the island produces roughly 10,000 STEM graduates annually from top-tier programs at NTU, NTHU, and NCTU, according to Taiwan's Ministry of Education statistics. Mid-level software engineers cost TWD 70,000–120,000/month (EUR 2,000–3,500) — significantly below Singapore and Hong Kong. The trade-off: Mandarin is the dominant working language, entity setup requires a local resident director, and IP enforcement, while improving, doesn't match Singapore or Hong Kong court precedents.


### How to Make the Call


Rank your priorities across five dimensions: talent cost, English proficiency, IP protection strength, entity setup speed, and timezone overlap with your EU HQ. No single jurisdiction wins on all five. In our experience at Branch8, we've helped EU clients land on Hong Kong when speed and financial structure mattered most, Singapore when the client needed to co-locate with enterprise APAC customers, and Taiwan when the engineering work was deeply technical and cost sensitivity was high.

## Step 2: Choose Your Employment Structure


The entity-versus-EOR decision determines your operational flexibility, cost structure, and legal exposure for years.


### Employer of Record (EOR) for Speed and Flexibility


An EOR like Deel, Remote, or Papaya Global lets you hire engineers in-jurisdiction without forming a legal entity. You can have your first APAC engineer onboarded within 2–3 weeks. Monthly per-employee fees range from USD 500–700 depending on the provider and jurisdiction. This model works well for teams under 15 people and when you need to validate the talent market before committing. The downside: you don't own the employment relationship directly, EOR contracts can limit your ability to offer equity compensation, and some jurisdictions (notably Taiwan) have grey areas around EOR legality that the National Taxation Bureau is increasingly scrutinizing.


### Subsidiary or Branch Office for Long-Term Commitment


If your plan calls for 20+ engineers within two years, a wholly-owned subsidiary typically makes more financial sense. In Hong Kong, incorporation costs run HKD 15,000–30,000 (EUR 1,800–3,600) through a corporate services provider, plus annual compliance costs of HKD 10,000–20,000. In Singapore, expect SGD 3,000–8,000 for incorporation and SGD 2,500–5,000 annually for a registered agent and compliance filings with ACRA. The entity gives you direct employment contracts, the ability to grant stock options under local schemes, and full control over IP assignment clauses.


### The Hybrid Approach We Recommend


At Branch8, we typically advise a staged approach: start with an EOR for months 1–6 while simultaneously incorporating a local entity. This lets you begin hiring immediately without waiting for entity registration, bank account approval, and MPF/CPF enrollment setup. When we helped a Hamburg-based SaaS company set up their Hong Kong engineering team in 2023, we used Deel as the interim EOR while our corporate services team completed the subsidiary incorporation in parallel. The first five engineers were onboarded via EOR within three weeks; by month four, all had transitioned to the subsidiary's payroll via Payroll2Me. Total time from decision to fully operational entity with 8 engineers: 14 weeks.


## Step 3: Build Your Talent Acquisition Pipeline


Hiring in APAC is a different sport than hiring in Berlin or Amsterdam. The rules of engagement, candidate expectations, and competitive dynamics vary sharply by market.


### Map the Competitive Landscape Before You Post a Single Role


In Singapore, you're competing with Google, Grab, Shopee, and a wave of US startups for the same senior engineers. LinkedIn's 2024 Talent Insights data shows that the median time-to-fill for a senior software engineer in Singapore is 62 days — nearly double the 34-day average in Taipei. In Hong Kong, the competitive set includes major banks' technology divisions (HSBC, Standard Chartered) and a growing number of Web3 companies. Know who you're up against and what they offer before you set compensation bands.


### Structure Compensation to Win in Each Market


APAC engineers evaluate offers differently than their EU counterparts. In Hong Kong and Singapore, base salary carries more weight than equity — partly because the startup ecosystem is younger and partly because housing costs demand cash. In Taiwan, engineers index heavily on work-life balance and learning opportunities. A practical compensation structure for a mid-level engineer in Hong Kong might look like: base HKD 45,000/month + 1–2 months bonus + equity (if your EU parent's stock option plan has a compliant APAC addendum) + medical insurance (mandatory MPF contributions are capped at HKD 1,500/month employer contribution).


### Leverage Local Recruiting Channels


Forget relying solely on LinkedIn. In Taiwan, top engineers congregate on PTT (the local forum), CakeResume, and Yourator. In Hong Kong, targeted outreach through local tech meetups (HK Tech Meetup, Codeaholics) and university partnerships with HKUST and HKU yields better signal-to-noise than job boards. In Singapore, NodeFlair and MyCareersFuture (the government-mandated portal for EP holders) are essential channels. Budget USD 3,000–6,000 per hire for agency fees if using local recruiters, or invest in an in-house talent acquisition contractor for the first six months.

## Step 4: Establish IP Protection and Legal Frameworks


This is where European companies have the most anxiety — and rightfully so. Your engineering hub will produce code, designs, and potentially patentable innovations. Every line of output needs clear ownership.


### IP Assignment Clauses in Employment Contracts


In all three jurisdictions, IP created during employment can be assigned to the employer, but the specifics matter. Hong Kong's Employment Ordinance and common law tradition make IP assignment straightforward — include explicit clauses in the employment contract and a separate IP assignment deed. Singapore follows a similar common law framework. Taiwan's Copyright Act defaults IP ownership to the creator unless explicitly assigned in writing, so your employment contracts must include comprehensive, attorney-reviewed assignment language covering all work product created during employment. Budget TWD 50,000–100,000 for a Taiwan IP attorney to draft compliant templates.


### Trade Secret Protections and Non-Compete Enforceability


Non-compete clauses are enforceable in Hong Kong and Singapore if they're reasonable in scope and duration (typically 6–12 months). In Taiwan, the Labor Standards Act amendments of 2015 set strict limits: non-competes must include compensation during the restriction period and cannot exceed two years. If your EU product involves proprietary algorithms or training data, layer your protection: NDAs at hiring, code repository access controls (we use GitLab's tiered permissions with audit logging), and regular IP audits.


### Structuring Cross-Border IP Holding


Many EU companies route APAC-generated IP through a holding structure — the APAC subsidiary assigns IP to the EU parent (or a Dutch or Irish holding company) via a licensing agreement. Transfer pricing rules apply: ensure the APAC entity receives arm's-length compensation for its R&D services. Hong Kong's Inland Revenue Department and Singapore's IRAS both have transfer pricing guidelines aligned with OECD standards. Get this wrong and you face double taxation. Get it right and you maintain clean IP chains that satisfy EU patent offices and due diligence in future funding rounds.


## Step 5: Set Up Operations and Development Infrastructure


Your APAC hub needs more than desks and laptops. The operational infrastructure determines whether your distributed engineering org functions as one team or fractures into silos.


### Workspace Strategy: Serviced Office vs. Dedicated Lease


For teams under 15, serviced offices (WeWork, The Executive Centre, JustCo) provide flexibility and speed. In Hong Kong, a hot desk runs HKD 3,000–5,000/month per person; dedicated desks cost HKD 5,000–8,000. In Singapore, comparable rates are SGD 500–900 per person. Once you exceed 15 engineers, a dedicated lease becomes cost-effective. In Taipei's Neihu Technology Park — the city's primary tech district — Grade A office space runs TWD 1,200–1,800 per ping (roughly EUR 12–18 per square metre), according to CBRE Taiwan's Q1 2024 market report.


### Development Toolchain and Access Management


Your APAC engineers need identical development environments to your EU team. This seems obvious but creates real friction. We've seen EU companies where the APAC team couldn't access internal tools because SSO was configured with IP-range restrictions tied to European office networks. Before day one, audit your toolchain: VPN configuration (we recommend Tailscale or WireGuard for split-tunnel setups), CI/CD pipeline access (ensure your GitHub Actions or GitLab CI runners don't have region-based rate limits), cloud console IAM roles, and Slack/Teams workspace permissions.



### Timezone Overlap and Async Collaboration Protocols


The UTC+8 to CET overlap is your operational lifeline. A Hong Kong or Singapore team working 9 AM–6 PM local overlaps with CET 2 PM–6 PM (winter) or 3 PM–6 PM (summer). That's a 3–4 hour window. Build your rituals around it: daily standups at 3 PM CET / 9 PM HKT (or shift the APAC team's hours slightly to 10 AM–7 PM for a better window). According to GitLab's 2024 Remote Work Report, distributed engineering teams that maintain at least 3 hours of daily synchronous overlap report 27% fewer merge request revision cycles than fully async teams.

## Step 6: Navigate Compliance and Ongoing Obligations


The setup is the sprint; compliance is the marathon. EU companies often underestimate ongoing regulatory obligations in APAC jurisdictions.


### Mandatory Benefits and Statutory Contributions


In Hong Kong, employers must contribute 5% of an employee's relevant income to the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF), capped at HKD 1,500/month. In Singapore, Central Provident Fund (CPF) employer contributions range from 17% for employees under 55 to lower rates for older workers — a significant cost that catches EU companies off guard. Taiwan's Labor Insurance and National Health Insurance employer contributions add approximately 15–18% on top of base salary. Factor these into your total cost modelling from day one.


### Annual Filings and Audit Requirements


Hong Kong subsidiaries must file annual returns with the Companies Registry and submit audited financial statements to the Inland Revenue Department. Singapore Pte Ltd companies file annual returns with ACRA and, if revenue exceeds SGD 10M, require a statutory audit. Taiwan branch offices have separate filing obligations with the Ministry of Economic Affairs. Budget USD 5,000–15,000 annually per jurisdiction for accounting and audit fees.


### Employment Law Nuances That Trip Up EU Companies


Hong Kong's Employment Ordinance mandates 7 days annual leave after 12 months of service (scaling to 14 days after 9 years) — far below EU standards. Most competitive employers offer 15–20 days to match market expectations. In Singapore, the Employment Act covers employees earning up to SGD 4,500/month for certain provisions, but most tech salaries exceed this threshold. Taiwan mandates a minimum of 3 days special leave in the first year, scaling to 30 days after 25 years of service. Align your leave policies with local market norms, not just legal minimums, or you'll lose talent to competitors offering more generous packages.


## Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them


After helping multiple EU companies set up APAC engineering operations, these are the patterns that consistently derail timelines and budgets.


### Mistake 1: Treating APAC as a Cost Centre Instead of a Product Team


The fastest way to kill morale and retention in your APAC hub is to position it as an outsourcing arm. Engineers in Singapore, Hong Kong, and Taipei have options — and they'll leave for companies that give them ownership over product decisions. Structure your APAC team around feature ownership or product domains, not ticket queues. According to a 2023 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, "impact of my work" ranked as the #2 factor for job satisfaction among APAC developers, behind only compensation.


### Mistake 2: Underestimating Bank Account Setup Timelines


In Hong Kong, opening a corporate bank account can take 2–6 weeks depending on the bank and your company's profile. HSBC and Standard Chartered have stricter KYC requirements for companies with no local directors. In Singapore, DBS and OCBC typically process applications in 1–3 weeks. EU companies frequently plan to run payroll by month two and then discover their bank account isn't active yet. Use the EOR bridge strategy described in Step 2 to decouple hiring timelines from banking timelines.


### Mistake 3: Ignoring Local Engineering Culture


German engineering culture prizes thoroughness and specification; Taiwanese engineering culture often favours rapid iteration. Neither is wrong, but if your EU engineering managers impose Berlin-style sprint planning on a Taipei team without adaptation, friction will follow. Invest in cultural onboarding — not a one-hour video, but a structured two-week programme where APAC engineers spend time (virtually or physically) with EU counterparts. We've seen this single practice reduce first-quarter attrition by over 40% across our client engagements.


### Mistake 4: Failing to Plan for Currency Exposure


You're paying salaries in HKD, SGD, or TWD while your revenue is likely in EUR. The HKD is pegged to the USD (within a narrow band managed by the HKMA), giving you USD exposure rather than direct EUR-HKD risk. SGD has appreciated roughly 8% against the EUR over the past three years, per European Central Bank reference rates. If your APAC payroll is USD 50,000/month, an unhedged 5% currency swing costs you EUR 30,000 annually. Use forward contracts or multi-currency accounts (Wise Business or HSBC GlobalView) to manage this exposure.

## Your EU Company APAC Engineering Hub Setup Guide: Decision Checklist


Use this checklist to validate your readiness before committing to execution:


- **Headcount plan** : 12-month and 36-month targets documented and approved by CTO and CFO
- **Jurisdiction selected** : Scored across cost, talent, IP protection, speed, and timezone overlap
- **Employment structure decided** : EOR, entity, or hybrid — with transition timeline if hybrid
- **Legal counsel engaged** : Local employment law and IP attorneys retained in target jurisdiction
- **Compensation benchmarks completed** : Using current salary data from Hays, Robert Half, or NodeFlair
- **IP framework drafted** : Assignment clauses, NDA templates, and cross-border holding structure reviewed
- **Toolchain audit done** : VPN, CI/CD, SSO, and cloud access verified for APAC network ranges
- **Banking timeline mapped** : Account applications submitted at least 6 weeks before first payroll date
- **Compliance calendar created** : MPF/CPF registration, annual filing deadlines, and audit schedules logged
- **Cultural onboarding programme designed** : Two-week structured programme, not a slide deck
